discoveries: (1) The red reasons, as seen. F1, both cases: the first call's check says "Containment: Acceptance test restored from HEAD: …/test_merged.py, …/test_new.py." (recorded `reverted`). It takes the combined test and the new test out of the index and the tree. The second call is then flagged "commit … a merge commit's own change to a ticket file or an acceptance test" for both tests, and `judge_commits` returns that finding. F2 and F3, all four cases: the live check is silent ("outcome=silent") and `judge_commits` returns `[]`. F4: the new path is flagged in one call and is a `judge_commits` finding; over two calls, both names are restored from HEAD. (2) In this git version (2.43), `git merge` names the moved-aside copy `<path>~HEAD` or `<path>~<branch>`, while `merge-tree` uses the name it was given (`<path>~<id>`); the guard accepts any `<path>~…`. (3) `test_w1_03_head_move_and_acceptance_test.py` is flaky on its own. A different set of cases fails on each run: 2, then 3 serially, then 4 in parallel. Every failure says "the fixture command `git commit -q --amend --no-edit …` did not move HEAD": an amend made in the same second as the commit it amends writes the identical commit. W1-03 imports nothing from W2-72, so my edits can't cause this.
risks: The hand-write cases only demand a finding at the commit when the committed test differs from git's own merge. That lets an implementation restore to git's own merge instead of HEAD; the call that makes the hand write must still catch it. The F2 and F3 cases accept a finding that names any path of the test: the old or new name, the directory's file, or `<path>~…`.
lessons: A two-call flow has to send PostToolUseFailure when `git merge` exits 1, as the harness does. Collect what both calls showed before asserting, so a red message shows both calls' text and findings. To drop a moved-aside copy, use `git rm` on the one unmerged path. Resolve a conflicted test with `git show <rev>:<path> >` rather than `git checkout --ours`, which fails once a restore has cleared the conflict stages.
